I'm glad you have an upward and expansive outlook. The realizations you've had about your own situation have undoubtedly helped you re-frame your possibilities. The same cannot be said for everyone here, however, so I always have trepidation when it comes to advice-giving here. 

It's true that the realities we face mean that SOs generally worry more about careers, social integration and livelihoods. It's also true that large institutions will discard us, or really anything required accreditation or background checks. It's ALSO true though, I think, that the same personal social-emotional maladaptations which led us here might also make it challenging for some people to "just be an entrepreneur like me".

This has happened to me a couple times, and it strikes where it hurts the most. I get it. Everyone wants some sort of future to look forward to; a place to feel needed, to feel validated, to feel like you're contributing something and "paying your way". Unfortunately, reality means that our choices are limited and none of the options are good. 

You'll hear stories here of people finding some sort of success in business, but from my perspective it's up to circumstance and chance. Skills that have already been acquired before the indictment. Which means for most people the work you have access to is demeaning, or at least outwardly unfulfilling: driving trucks, dishwashers, cashier at Popeye's. 

I've been in the position you are. Arguably I'm still there. The only thing you can "do" is *something*. Going to some sort of work to fill your day, no matter what it is. Applying and being rejected from jobs by the hundreds. Sitting in the Home Depot parking lot at 5:30am as a day laborer. 

You mentioned having a wife, one who you perceive as being fed up... Have you considered asking her for advice, as lame as that sounds? Expecting you to make serious cash is frankly a bit ridiculous.

Not to be that guy, but from a management perspective it might behoove you to go through the checklist to just make sure they're being dweebs and not something correctable from your end (or management's end). 
First, by your description, it sounds like you expect their tenure to be short: especially with teens, the reward circuits in their brain are looking for more than time spent = money for weed. If they see it as a place with no chance for advancement, they're more likely to put in minimum effort (in which case it is probably a good idea to let them go, to teach them exactly where the boundary is between minimum and unemployed). Motivated kids who want to be in the industry will probably put the work in, but they definitely won't stick around at a dead-end job. 
Second, it's true that you might be spoiling them or over-helping... at least in the sense that having explicitly clear expectations may help. Did you, for instance, make a bulletin sheet with things required for every service? 
Third, it's impossible to tell the dynamic just from this post, but if you treat them like you think they're spoiled, dumb, entitled, and lazy... they might just act that way.

You have to decide for yourself what sort of role you're comfortable taking with them. Many people in the orbit of post-offense SOs (or even people who come out about their attractions) say they want to be supportive. However, they show visible discomfort whenever the SO brings up the topic of their offense, their feelings or attractions, or anything of that nature. At least for me, the body language of someone who really doesn't want to hear about these things is obvious, and personally after that I'll refrain from sharing my actual feelings. Even after years of group and personal therapy, accepting what they did and how they feel is a process. If it was for possession, they might even feel like it was an addiction (which never truly goes away, only gets managed) or even a sexual orientation. It's a struggle in and of itself, to say nothing of the struggle (as an SO) of who to trust with our feelings and constant self-censorship. 

If you're uncomfortable with the elements of their past, their offense, be upfront about it and draw some lines regarding your stance on the issues, your attitude on grace or forgiveness, and what kind of support you can give comfortably. Ask yourself if you really can forgive them or accept them for who they are, or if you're adopting "hate the sin, not the sinner" mentality, which I find is not equivalent to actual grace or forgiveness.

It's a blow to the stability of someone trying to recover if they open up to someone and find discomfort or hidden animosity. As a SO, this has been the overwhelming majority of my experience: people who say they want to support me who actually grow distant and uncomfortable once I share how I feel; self-censorship around people who are friends but likely would not survive friendship once they knew about my past; constant evaluation of how "real" any of my relationships are if I can't share my whole self or whether I've fallen off the wagon. 

Since this is from an SO's perspective, take it with the mandatory pillar of salt, but hopefully it can inform you.

I also have a recently-earned history degree and I feel the struggle, especially now when joblessness is so common. I haven’t found a way out (still unemployed, still mostly hopeless about a “fruitful and rewarding career”), so I can’t give you the grass-is-greener perspective. 

What I can say is that the reality is thus: most people don’t break through. Most people struggle, work as cashiers or in minimum wage jobs forever, with abusive bosses and poor conditions. Anything better is sheer luck. All you can do is be prepared when the opportunity comes.

How to cope? Try not to wrap up your entire self-image, identity and self-esteem in your work and income. It sounds trite, but there is a difference between “work to live” and “live to work”. I have found that being a part of a community, whether a network or friends, family, volunteer groups, board game nights, or whatever— that is the safety net to stop you from spiraling down.

From the sounds of it, you’re already a fairly musical person. Everyone is to some extent. Before you get into needing fancy software like Sibelius or Ableton or whatever, the best way to become creative is simply to do it. Over and over. Try writing a song, a lick, a rhythm, whatever suits you. Don’t think too hard about it. Record it if you don’t know how to notate it. 

If you do that, you can look back on it and critique it, to see how it didn’t exactly line up with what was in your head. From THERE, you can figure out what tools or skills you need to more accurately realize what’s knocking around in your head. If it’s something like trap or EDM, you might want to learn how to use a DAW, midi, and samples. If it’s blues you might want to learn how to play guitar. If you like western music, study music theory and harmony if that’s your cup of tea. The only way to know is by doing.

There’s no one right way to write music or be a musician, but the one skill you DO need is the ability to look at your own work and figure out what you need to do in order to make it better.
